title: Automated Verification of Hamiltonian Simulation by Quantum Signal Processing
authors: Min Lai, Yu-Fang Chen, Shih-Han Hung
abstract: We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first fully automated verification framework for QSP-based Hamiltonian simulation. Our framework exploits the structure of the simulation algorithm: Hamiltonians are given as weighted sums of Pauli strings, embedded into larger unitaries through block encodings, and transformed into time-evolution operators by quantum signal processing (QSP). Using a symbolic Pauli-sum semantics for ancilla-indexed circuit blocks, our verifier proves that the distinguished all-zero ancilla block is proportional to the target Hamiltonian and infers the subnormalization factor automatically. It then verifies the QSP layer by extracting the implemented polynomial transformation and certifying its approximation error. This structure-aware abstraction is essential for scalability. Composing our verified block encoding and QSP wrapper yields an estimated macro-expanded size of about 1.52 million gates. The verifier certifies the block encoding once and checks the QSP layer through its abstract interface, without expanding the oracle calls. Our implementation verifies block encodings of structured Pauli-sum Hamiltonians with up to 256 system qubits and verifies QSP Hamiltonian-simulation instances by extracting their implemented polynomials and checking the resulting approximation bounds. These results show that fully automated verification can handle common Hamiltonian-simulation circuits at substantial scale when it exploits their algorithmic structure.
summary: This paper introduces the first fully automated verification framework for Hamiltonian simulation circuits built using Quantum Signal Processing (QSP). The framework works by structurally analyzing the circuit in two parts: verifying the block encoding of the Hamiltonian and certifying the polynomial approximation implemented by the QSP layer. This allows for rigorous, scalable verification of complex quantum algorithms without needing to simulate the entire, potentially massive, circuit.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing a fully automated and scalable verification framework for quantum circuits used to simulate time evolution governed by a Hamiltonian.
main_result: They present a structure-aware verifier that can certify the correctness of QSP-based Hamiltonian simulations for large systems (up to 256 qubits) by analyzing the block encoding and QSP layer abstractly.
method: The verification framework combines symbolic Pauli-sum semantics with structural analysis to certify two components: the block encoding (proving proportionality to the target Hamiltonian) and the QSP layer (extracting and bounding the implemented polynomial transformation).
model_or_system: The model is quantum computation, specifically simulating the time evolution operator $e^{-iHt}$ for a Hamiltonian $H$ expressed as a weighted sum of Pauli strings. The simulation relies on block encoding techniques and Quantum Signal Processing (QSP).
key_observables: The primary observables are the error bound ($\epsilon$) on the approximation of the time-evolution operator and the estimated macro-expanded circuit size.
important_parameters: System qubit count (up to 256), approximation error $\epsilon$, and the structure of the Pauli-sum Hamiltonian.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the Hamiltonian $H$ is structured as a Pauli-sum and that the QSP approximation is valid over the spectral range of the Hamiltonian.
figures_summary: The notes reference figures illustrating the block encoding of specific Hamiltonians (like $X-Z$) and the general structure of the QSP circuit implementation.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the two-part verification process (block encoding certification and QSP layer certification), demonstrates its application to large-scale benchmarks, and discusses its advantages over general verification tools.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial tool for quantum algorithm development by moving beyond simple circuit simulation to provide rigorous, automated guarantees about the fidelity of complex, structure-dependent quantum operations like Hamiltonian simulation.
